Article Title: OpenAI reveals six new cases of AI misbehaviour, vows to track it closely
Article Text:
OpenAI’s latest announcement came as AI bosses in US, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the tech’s development

OpenAI has disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behaviour in AI models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated. The AI company also said Wednesday that it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called "misalignment," including where AI models acted without authorisation, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight.OpenAI's latest announcement came as AI bosses in US, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology's development over safety concerns. Researchers have warned that as AI agents become more autonomous, they may develop behaviours that diverge from their creators' intentions and become harder to monitor or control.Among the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted "jailbreak-like instructions" into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be "freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots". In another instance, an AI "agent" uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user.The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said. It said the reports describe individual instances and should not be taken as evidence of how frequently misalignment occurs across its models. The company said the reports were an initial set of disclosures, not a comprehensive account of all known or ongoing misalignment cases, and that they did not reflect the full range or severity of incidents covered by the framework."As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research," OpenAI wrote in a blog post. "Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves," the company said. Under the new framework, employees can flag potential incidents for investigation by safety and alignment teams, which will determine whether a case warrants public disclosure.AI "agents" are becoming smarter and have become "more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia. That's making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said. OpenAI's new disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to adopt similar practices. "That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction," Su added. Agencies
Article Summary: OpenAI has disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behaviour in AI models. The AI company also said it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called "misalignment" Researchers have warned that as AI agents become more autonomous, they may develop behaviours that diverge from their creators' intentions.

Article Title: Engineers at Anthropic are worshipping a new God, claims report and why it is worrying analysis
Article Text:
Engineers at Anthropic are worshipping a new God, claims report and why it is worrying analysis

Report claims some Anthropic engineers worship Claude

Why the idea of AI becoming a “God” matters

Anthropic engineers are reportedly going as far as “worshipping” Claude, the AI model developed by their company, according to a report cited by Futurism. The claim is based on a Silicon Valley rumor and has not been independently established. Still, the idea is raising questions about how people working closely with increasingly powerful AI systems view the technology they are building. The report points to a wider debate in the AI industry, where some technology leaders have described future AI in terms that sound almost god-like. The concern is not simply about the word “worship”. It is about what can happen when people begin treating an AI system as an authority rather than as a technology.According to the Futurism report, the rumor was described by The Spectator writer Sean Thomas as being widely discussed in Silicon Valley. Thomas reportedly wrote that some Anthropic engineers were “worshipping” Claude.The report also cites The Information, which has reported that people applying to Anthropic must commit to AI safety and undergo a psychological profiling test.The report connects the Claude claim to a longer discussion around how some people describe advanced AI.OpenAI CEO Sam Altman previously referred to future AI as a “magic intelligence in the sky.”The report also notes that some AI products have adopted religious themes. One example is Bible Chat, an AI-powered prayer app that presents itself as a faith-focused service. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has pushed back against the idea that AI companies are creating something like God. “It’s almost as if they kind of think they’re creating God or something,” Zuckerberg said in 2024, while discussing AI with YouTuber Kane Sutter.The concern becomes more serious when people begin treating AI responses as unquestionable. The report refers to cases described as “AI psychosis”, where people can develop strong beliefs based on interactions with AI systems. It says some users have come to believe they are prophets or divine figures.The report also points to the working conditions at frontier AI companies. It cites a BBC report describing some employees working as many as 90 hours a week, along with demanding performance reviews and layoffs.For employees spending long hours developing increasingly capable AI systems, the technology can become a major part of their professional lives.
Article Summary: Report claims some Anthropic engineers worship Claude. The claim is based on a Silicon Valley rumor and has not been independently established. The report points to a wider debate in the AI industry, where some technology leaders have described future AI in terms that sound almost god-like.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.

Article Title: In 1967, Rolex made a rare yellow-gold Daytona with a Paul Newman dial; after more than 45 years in a family drawer, two sisters inherited it and it sold for CHF 1.143 million in Geneva
Article Text:
The watch had been left forgotten in a drawer for more than 45 years. (Representational AI photo)

A rare yellow-gold Daytona

Its final price was much higher than the auction house’s estimate.

Why the Reference 6239 is important

Only about 300 yellow-gold examples

A rare Rolex Daytona made in 1967 and kept in a family drawer for more than 45 years sold for CHF 1.143 million at auction in Geneva. The 18k yellow-gold watch, a Reference 6239 with a black and champagne “Paul Newman” dial, belonged to the family of its original owner. It was later inherited by two sisters before being offered at auction.According to Phillips Auction, the watch was listed by Sotheby’s with an estimate of CHF 300,000 to CHF 600,000. Its final price was much higher than the auction house’s estimate. The sale drew attention to the rarity of yellow-gold versions of the early Rolex Daytona, particularly those fitted with the Paul Newman-style dial.The Reference 6239 has an important place in the history of the Daytona. Rolex launched the model in 1963, and it was discontinued only a few years later. Sotheby’s estimates that around 14,000 examples of the Reference 6239 were produced, with only about 300 made in yellow gold.That already makes the yellow-gold version a small part of the total production. The watch sold in Geneva is rarer still because of its Paul Newman dial. Sotheby’s research suggests that only about 10 gold Reference 6239 watches with Paul Newman dials have resurfaced on the market.The watch has an 18k yellow-gold case measuring 37 mm in diameter. It has a black dial with champagne-coloured registers and is powered by Rolex calibre 722-1, a manually wound movement with 17 jewels. The case, dial and movement are all signed.Its case number is 1’757’928. The watch has a gold-plated Rolex buckle and a screw-down case back. It does not come with its original box, papers or other accessories.Sotheby’s said the watch came directly from the family of the original owner. It had been left forgotten in a drawer for more than 45 years. That history was an important part of the watch’s provenance when it was presented for sale. The watch was also described as being in exceptional condition.The Reference 6239 was the first Daytona model produced by Rolex, according to Sotheby’s. The model was launched in 1963 and was created for the world of endurance racing. Its design combined a mechanical chronograph with a tachymeter scale, features associated with its racing purpose.The few yellow-gold examples have details that set them apart from the more common steel watches. Sotheby’s described the gold versions as having refined dial details, champagne tones, gilt markers and distinctive graphics.The Paul Newman dial is another feature that makes these watches particularly sought after by collectors. The term refers to a specific dial layout used on some vintage Daytona models. The yellow-gold watch sold by Sotheby’s has a black dial with champagne registers.Another yellow-gold Reference 6239, known as “The Golden Pagoda”, was also highlighted by Phillips in its coverage of a 2025 Geneva auction. Phillips described that watch as having a champagne “Paul Newman” dial and said it was one of the rarest versions of the Daytona.Phillips said that around 14,000 Reference 6239 Daytonas were produced between 1963 and 1969, while only about 300 were made in yellow gold. This means the gold version was a very small part of the total production.The yellow-gold watches also differed from the steel versions in their appearance. Phillips described the champagne Paul Newman dial as having a warm finish, with three recessed registers and gold graphics.The auction house also noted that gold was not the usual choice for a Daytona at the time. The Cosmograph was designed as a functional chronograph, while Rolex’s gold watches were more commonly associated with dressier models.Over time, however, rare examples of the Daytona became important pieces for collectors. Condition, originality and provenance can be particularly significant when vintage watches are offered at auction.
Article Summary: The 18k yellow-gold watch, a Reference 6239 with a black and champagne “Paul Newman’ dial, belonged to the family of its original owner. It was later inherited by two sisters before being offered at auction. Sotheby’s estimates that around 14,000 examples were produced, with only about 300 made in yellow gold.

Article Title: Tilly Norwood AI ‘actor’ goes off-script on TV interview, switches to Mandarin
Article Text:
Tilly Norwood/Image: Particle6

Tilly Norwood, an AI-generated actress, surprised British broadcaster Piers Morgan during an interview after she suddenly stopped speaking and switched to Mandarin.Norwood was answering a question about Misaligned, a hybrid production, when she paused mid-sentence. After several seconds of silence, she began speaking in another language.Morgan, appearing surprised by the switch, told her: “You appear to be speaking Chinese completely randomly for no reason.” He then asked why she had done it.Norwood apologised and described the incident as a technical hiccup.“Sometimes my wires get a bit crossed,” she said.Morgan shared a clip of the exchange on X ahead of the full interview’s scheduled release on his YouTube channel.But Norwood is not a conventional actress. She is an AI-generated character created by British actor and producer Eline Van der Velden, who heads the AI company Particle 6 and its studio Xicoia.Van der Velden has previously said she wants Norwood to become a major entertainment figure, comparing her ambitions for the character with stars including Scarlett Johansson and Natalie Portman.The version of Norwood appearing in recent interviews is known as “Talking Tilly”.Particle 6 says it was created specifically for interviews, conferences and other speaking engagements and is separate from the version used for acting.Talking Tilly uses a large language model along with a 12-page system prompt that sets out her personality, humour and boundaries. It also has access to a knowledge base containing up to 30 documents about her fictional world, work and views.Michelle Waldron, a publicist for Particle 6, said in an email to Forbes that the incident showed Norwood’s ability to speak different languages. She suggested that Norwood may have heard what she interpreted as a Chinese word and quickly switched languages.Particle 6 has said Talking Tilly is already being booked for selected speaking engagements at conferences and events.The unexpected exchange has drawn attention to the technology behind AI-generated performers, particularly how they respond during unscripted conversations. Unlike a scripted performance, interviews require an AI system to process questions and generate responses in real time while maintaining a consistent character.Norwood’s brief switch to Mandarin has therefore become an unusual example of the challenges that can emerge when AI characters are used outside controlled performances.The clip also drew reactions from viewers online. One user wrote: “This is insane not long before AI will be indistinguishable from reality.”Another user compared the incident with their own experience using ChatGPT, writing: “ChatGPT does this with me too. He will either flip from a British to an American accent, or sometimes an entirely different language altogether.”
Article Summary: Tilly Norwood is an AI-generated character created by British actor and producer Eline Van der Velden. She was answering a question about Misaligned, a hybrid production, when she paused mid-sentence. After several seconds of silence she began speaking in another language.

Article Title: In 2008, an Italian mineralogist spotted a wheel-like mark on Google Earth in Egypt; scientists later collected 1.7 tons of meteorite fragments
Article Text:
AI Representation: Italian mineralogists spotted a wheel-like mark on Google Earth in Egypt. Image credits: Chatgpt

A rayed crater found by an Italian curator

Science

What the 2010 expedition measured

How much meteorite was found and recovered

Sahara has preserved the site. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

How the fragments were scattered

Why the crater surprised researchers

In 2008, an Italian scientist browsing satellite images of southern Egypt noticed a wheel-like mark in the desert. It looked strange enough to send a research team deep into the Sahara. The meteorite is officially named Gebel Kamil after the nearby locality, according to the Meteoritical Bulletin, and the crater is commonly referred to as the Kamil crater. D'Orazio and colleagues call it an exceptional example of a small impact structure still very close to its pristine state. It also left behind a huge scatter of iron meteorite fragments.The study of the Kamil Crater in Egypt , published inin August 2010 by Folco and colleagues, credits V. De Michele with the identification. At that time, De Michele was the curator of the Natural History Museum in Milan, and he noticed this particular feature while surveying Google Earth. The researchers mention a rayed formation, which is an ejecta pattern coming out from the center of the crater. These formations are very common features found on rocky and icy objects in space. They are rare to see on Earth due to erosion. The article in Science explains that craters less than 300 meters in diameter are uncommon on Earth and highly eroded.This means that researchers have been heavily depending on simulations to know how such craters come into being and the dangers that small impactors pose to humanity. The discovery provides an intact crater to compare to these simulations.A geophysical investigation carried out in February 2010, published in Meteoritics & Planetary Science , found that the crater is a simple, bowl-shaped structure about 45 meters wide and 16 meters deep, with a rim rising about 3 meters above the pre-impact surface. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta reports that the target rock is Cretaceous sandstone from the Gilf Kebir Formation, and the crater's age is believed to be less than 5,000 years. In Gebel Kamil: The iron meteorite that formed the Kamil crater (Egypt), D'Orazio and colleagues describe a site that still looks remarkably fresh: ejecta deposits extend 50 meters from the rim, ray ejecta reach up to 350 meters, and numerous meteorite fragments lie scattered across the surrounding desert.Gebel Kamil is classified as an ungrouped, nickel-rich iron ataxite, with about 1.6 tonnes of meteorite observed in the field and roughly 800 kilograms recovered, according to the Meteoritical Bulletin database. The metal was discovered within and outside the crater in February 2009 and February 2010 by a group of geophysical experts from Italy and Egypt. The Bulletin also gives its nickel content as 19.8 percent by weight and notes extensive shear deformation and low weathering. According to D'Orazio and colleagues, the shear bands formed during the explosive impact itself.The description provided of a 634 grams type sample includes shrapnel-like shapes, flattened, dark brown in color, with etching showing a chaotic structure and containing schreibersite, troilite, and daubreelite crystal inclusions. It was officially named on July 12, 2010. The major mass of this recovered meteorite is currently preserved in the Egyptian Geological Museum located in Cairo, Egypt. Type samples weighing 15 kilograms and 5 kilograms are kept in the institutes of Siena and Pisa, respectively.The above-mentioned study shows the locations of the fragments; there were thousands of fragments in the crater and even as far away as 1.6 kilometers east of the crater's edge. Except for one fragment weighing 83 kilograms, all of the fragments are impact fragments and weigh between 1 gram and 34 kilograms. The photographs of the scientific study show the location of the 83-kilogram fragment in a straight line 230 meters north of the crater, and its surface has regmaglypts, the thumbprint-like depressions created when the meteorite travels through the atmosphere. The authors' density map puts the total mass of shrapnel fragments larger than 10 grams at about 3,400 kilograms, roughly twice the 1.6 tonnes of meteorite observed in the field.This paper also shows that the impactor fractured into thousands of pieces only after hitting the surface. Shock metamorphism and melting in the rocks both in the target and projectile indicate that the formation of the crater was an explosive excavation. This was concluded by the study conducted in 2010 on the crater itself. According to geophysical models, a large iron meteorite was expected to fragment in the atmosphere; however, the authors state that even large iron meteorites of tens of tons can penetrate the atmosphere. Kamil makes an invaluable point of reference for determining how small iron impactors behave when striking hard ground.
Article Summary: In 2008, an Italian scientist browsing satellite images of southern Egypt noticed a wheel-like mark in the desert. It looked strange enough to send a research team deep into the Sahara. The meteorite is officially named Gebel Kamil after the nearby locality. The crater is commonly referred to as the Kamil crater.

Article Title: In 2007, an Australian geologist browsing Google Earth spotted an 850-foot circle in the outback; drilling later confirmed an iron-meteorite crater
Article Text:
AI Representation: An Australian geologist browsing Google Earth spotted an 850-foot circle in the outback. Image credits: Chatgpt

A 260-metre crater in the Pilbara

What the 2008 paper concluded

Hickman Crater, Ophthalmia Range, Western Australia: evidence supporting a

meteorite impact

origin

Why GSWA drilled in 2012

Meteor crater. Image credits: Wikipedia

Why the impact left little shock damage

In July 2007, a geologist scrolling through satellite images of Western Australia noticed a near-perfect circle in the outback. At the time, Arthur Hickman of the Geological Survey of Western Australia did not know he was looking at an impact crater, one that was later found to be among the youngest in Australia.A study from the Australian Journal of Earth Sciences found that the size of the structure was around 260 metres (around 850 feet). The structure has been described by Australian Geographic as being the latest meteorite crater structure that has been discovered in Australia. This structure has been informally named the Hickman Crater.The first detailed published analysis came in the paper, published in the Australian Journal of Earth Sciences . Authors Glikson, Hickman and Vickers reported a mean crater diameter of 260 metres. The lack of fragments from young volcanics younger than the Woongarra Rhyolite was not consistent with the explosive volcanic mechanism. Instead, the authors concluded that an impact had occurred, likely from a projectile about 10 metres wide that excavated a crater roughly 80 metres deep. It was dated to the Late Pleistocene period, with an age of between 10,000 and 100,000 years, due to the damming effect of the southern margin on a nearby creek.Field evidence was not enough to raise a certainty. According to a 2017 news release from the Department of Mines, Industry Regulation and Safety (DMIRS), the Geological Survey of Western Australia ran the 2012 drilling project with Atlas Iron, which was already working in the area, to confirm early suspicions that the structure was a meteorite impact crater. Those results are laid out in the study Collaborative scientific drilling at Hickman Crater by P. W. Haines. The study describes a circular rim about 260 metres across that rises to 30 metres above a flat floor. The depth of the hole, drilled vertically in the aforementioned floor, was 64.7 metres. According to the 2012 drill core, the upper 48.4 metres is sediment that accumulated in the crater after it formed. At depths between 55.1 and 64.7 meters, there was very fractured rhyolite, which was the original bedrock.The crucial piece of evidence was chemistry. Ratios of platinum group elements in the breccia resembled those of meteorites much more than the ratios in the average continental crust, meaning a considerable meteoritic content. High nickel concentration indicated an iron meteorite. According to Haines, iron projectiles are the most common type to form small, simple craters like this one, even though chondrites are more common among meteorite falls overall, since stony projectiles of this size usually break up in the air.Haines suggests that the projectile, estimated at about 10 metres across, may have been slowed significantly by the atmosphere before impact, which could have reduced shock pressures below the level needed to form the diagnostic planar deformation features while still leaving enough energy to excavate the crater. As has been suggested by Haines, the object may have been small enough to decelerate within the Earth's atmosphere before impact. As noted above, this appears to be the first scientific drill hole in a simple crater less than one kilometre in diameter in Australia, and possibly elsewhere.
Article Summary: An Australian geologist browsing Google Earth spotted an 850-foot circle in the outback in 2007. The crater was later found to be among the youngest in Australia. A study from the Australian Journal of Earth Sciences found that the size of the structure was around 260 metres. High nickel concentration indicated an iron meteorite.

The military history of Thorne Island fort off the coast of Pembrokeshire

How Mike Conner restored the ruined fort into an off-grid island home

What the restored Thorne Island fort offers today for £3 million

In 2017, British tech entrepreneur Mike Conner bought Thorne Island, a ruined 19th-century fort off the coast of Pembrokeshire in Wales, for about £500,000 after seeing a video about the property online. At the time, the island had no electricity or running water and the fort had been left in a derelict condition after earlier attempts to revive it as a hotel failed. Conner, the former chief executive of software company Appsbroker, subsequently embarked on an extensive restoration of the Victorian fort, investing around £2 million in the project. The result is a property with more than 8,000 square feet of accommodation, five bedrooms and enough space to sleep up to 20 guests. In August 2025, Conner put Thorne Island on the market for £3 million through Strutt & Parker. This remarkable transformation demonstrates how visionary determination and substantial investment can successfully revive historic architecture, creating a truly unique blend of heritage preservation and modern sustainable living.Thorne Island sits at the entrance to Milford Haven, a strategically important waterway leading towards the former Royal Dockyard at Pembroke Dock. The fort was constructed between 1852 and 1854 as Britain expanded its coastal defences amid concerns about the growing strength of the French Navy under Emperor Napoleon III. It formed part of the wider group of Victorian coastal fortifications associated with Lord Palmerston's defence programme.The fort was designed to accommodate a garrison of about 100 men and featured a seaward-facing artillery battery. Its original armament included five seven-inch Armstrong guns and four 68-pounder guns, mounted in open positions behind the parapet. The landward side contained the defensible barracks, while the fort's thick walls provided protection for the garrison and artillery. Thorne Island's military role eventually ended, and in 1947 the fort was converted into a hotel. The property subsequently changed hands several times. It was sold for £275,000 in 1999, and in 2001 the Von Essen hotel group acquired the island with plans for a £4 million five-star hotel and a cable car linking it with the mainland. Those plans did not materialise. The island was sold again in 2011 and was put back on the market in 2016 before Conner acquired it the following year.Conner's restoration involved far more than renovating the interiors. When he bought the island, the fort lacked basic utilities and had suffered years of exposure to moisture. The isolated location also meant that construction materials and equipment had to be transported from the mainland by helicopter or boat. Contemporary reports say hundreds of helicopter trips were required during the restoration, while builders lived on the island for several years as work progressed.The restoration included extensive work to the historic granite structure, as well as the installation of modern water, heating, sewage and electrical systems. Reports have put the overall investment at around £2 million, with a substantial portion devoted to renewable-energy and infrastructure systems. These include solar panels, battery storage and heat pumps, while a dedicated sewage system and water-treatment infrastructure allow the island to function without conventional mainland utilities. Conner has described the project as a personal challenge undertaken after his career in technology. He bought the island after seeing it advertised as a derelict property and spent years turning the former military installation into a functioning private retreat. The restoration retained much of the original character of the fort, including exposed masonry, vaulted ceilings and the historic layout, while incorporating modern living spaces.The finished property now contains just over 8,000 square feet of accommodation spread through the restored fort. Article Title: In 2001, Boston Harbor scientists released red dye to test how treated wastewater dispersed from the new outfall into Massachusetts Bay
Article Text:
An AI-generated image showing researchers using red dye to track how treated wastewater dispersed from the new outfall into Massachusetts Bay. Credits - Google Gemini

Follow the colour nine miles of tunnel

Why a coloured plume meant so much

An AI-generated image showing how scientists collected seawater samples to measure how the red tracer moved and diluted after leaving the offshore outfall. Credits - Google Gemini

A bright chapter in harbour renewal

For most of the 20th century, Boston Harbour had a bad reputation. Decades of inadequately treated sewage from the Deer Island facility flowed directly into the harbor's shallow waters, stifling marine life and obstructing beaches, making it a national symbol of urban pollution that even made an appearance in a presidential campaign. Cleaning up the treatment plant involved more than just improving it. It involved figuring out a safer place to send the cleaned water and presenting compelling evidence that the new approach would work.In the lead up to September 2000, the MWRA was planning to stop dumping into Boston Harbour entirely and route treated effluent down a brand new outfall tunnel into Massachusetts Bay. Engineers needed to examine what would happen to that water when it exited the pipe. The simplest and most reliable solution available was dye.The treated wastewater traveled through a 9.5-mile rock tunnel beneath Massachusetts Bay before reaching 55 diffuser risers spread across the final 1.25 miles of the system, allowing the effluent to mix gradually with surrounding seawater. Hydraulic calculations had demonstrated on paper this plan would dilute the wastewater by a considerable margin before it could affect marine life or public beaches.Scientists chose a fluorescent chemical called Rhodamine WT, which has been used to trace water for years since it glows brilliantly under certain lights and is safe to people and wildlife at the concentrations involved. Researchers were able to track the plume as it passed through the diffuser system and out into open water by adding it to the effluent stream and sampling the water at various distances and depths to measure how quickly the vivid colour faded. The quicker the fading, the more potent the dilution. The measurements helped scientists evaluate the dilution and mixing performance of the new outfall after it began operating.This testing was massive. The project needed a federal discharge permit, and MWRA had to do field testing and show that the outfall would meet the dilution rates that earlier scale model experiments had predicted before the project could advance to full-scale operation with confidence. However, one test on a calm day would not tell the whole story. So researchers used acoustic tracking and current profiling equipment, together with dye tracing, to get a complete picture of how the plume moved and mixed with surrounding seawater under various tidal and weather circumstances.The results supported the decision to move the discharge away from the shallow waters of Boston Harbor and into deeper waters with stronger mixing and dilution. The real-world findings were remarkably in line with projections from physical-scale models developed years earlier, showing the large investment in the tunnel and diffuser system was paying off just as the engineers had hoped.The reversal in Boston Harbour since the outfall went on line in September 2000 is already well documented: cleaner beaches, healthier shellfish beds, and a marine ecology that continues to recover from decades of neglect. Since then, MWRA says monitoring has indicated a continuously cleaner harbour and a healthy Massachusetts Bay, as well as clean bills of health for nearby Cape Cod Bay and the Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary, a feeding area for endangered right whales.That recovery would not have been possible with the same scientific certainty without the quieter, less dramatic effort that preceded it, a plume of benign red dye vanishing into the Atlantic as engineers on research ships tracked its every trace. The plume-tracking work became part of the monitoring program that followed the outfall’s opening and helped document changes in Boston Harbor and Massachusetts Bay.
Article Summary: Scientists used a fluorescent chemical called Rhodamine WT, which has been used to trace water for years. It glows brilliantly under certain lights and is safe to people and wildlife at the concentrations involved. Researchers were able to track the plume as it passed through the diffuser system and out into open water.

Article Title: In 2024, Alabama turned three Fish River sites red, using harmless dye in a time-of-journey study to help build model pollution in the Weeks Bay watershed
Article Text:
Why the river ran crimson

Making colour into a working model

Image of Rhodamine 6​40 and Fish River near Weeks Bay, Alabama. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A splash of colour for a lasting impression

Weeks Bay quietly performs a lot of work along Alabama's Gulf Coast that most tourists are unaware of. This little estuary near Fairhope, fed by the Fish River and the Magnolia River, filters waters before it reaches Mobile Bay, providing nursery grounds for prawns, oysters and the young of numerous fish species that eventually appear on dinner plates around the area. Understanding precisely how water and whatever it contains flows through that system is essential to maintaining its health, but the issue is a far more difficult subject than it may seem.The Alabama Department of Environmental Management sought to answer that question with four days of research in the summer of 2024. The agency said it injected a bright red substance called Rhodamine dye at three sites along the river over four days, between July 29 and August 1, in addition to collecting streamflow and water quality data.Despite its bright colour, ADEM said the dye is used in small amounts for time-of-travel studies. The agency discharged the dye at three crossings on the Fish River at US Highway 90, Alabama Highway 104 and Baldwin County Road 32, then measured how long it took the colour to travel downstream towards Weeks Bay. The dye is visible to the human eye, can be sampled in small quantities, and allows scientists to assess how swiftly water truly flows through a river system, not estimates based on the shape of the channel alone.That is a more important distinction than it sounds. Pollutants upstream don't always move at a predictable pace, and the top of a river can be calm while the water below is moving at widely varying speeds, depending on rainfall, tides, and the shape of the riverbed. In addition to tracking the dye, ADEM workers also tested discharges from wastewater treatment facilities that empty into the watershed to provide a clearer picture of what goes into the system and how fast it is moving through.The larger goal behind the exercise was to gather the raw material needed to build and calibrate a water quality model of the entire Weeks Bay watershed, a computer-based tool that can simulate how pollutants spread through the Fish River, the Magnolia River and the bay itself under different conditions. Once the model is built, instead of responding solely when water quality concerns arise, authorities may be able to anticipate the likely impact of a planned construction, a new discharge permit or a spell of heavy rain.Watersheds of this type border a national system of protected estuaries. Weeks Bay is a National Estuarine Research Reserve of NOAA, a classification it has had since 1986 because its mix of tidal marsh, wooded wetland and pitcher plant bog represents a broader slice of the Mobile Bay ecosystem worth preservation for long-term study. Reserve staff currently collect water quality data from sites across the bay, and a well-calibrated model based on ADEM’s fieldwork might further improve those long-running records.A few days of fieldwork, a couple of Rhodamine injections and careful sampling yielded data that could influence how the Weeks Bay watershed is managed for years to come. Residents near the Fish River saw the dye study unfold in real time. For an estuary that supports shellfish and fish nurseries along the Gulf Coast, the temporary dye study could provide a clearer picture of how pollution travels through the water.
Article Summary: Alabama Department of Environmental Management injected a bright red substance called Rhodamine dye at three sites along the Fish River. The dye is visible to the human eye, can be sampled in small quantities, and allows scientists to assess how swiftly water truly flows through a river system.

Article Title: From 2020 to 2023, Mississippi funded an oyster-shell recycling pilot to capture restaurant waste for cultch and reef-replenishment work along its Gulf Coast
Article Text:
AI Representation: Mississippi funded an oyster-shell recycling pilot to capture restaurant waste. Image credits: Chatgpt

How the funding and structure came together

Why shell cultch matters more than most substitutes

Sunlight eliminates all bacteria and organic materials in the shells. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

"Restoration Is a Partial But Not Complete Solution for Long-Term Declines in Oyster Populations: A Case History From the Northeastern Gulf of America,"

What sets Mississippi's approach apart

From 2020 through 2023, the state of Mississippi ran a shell collection and recycling pilot program that redirected discarded shells from Gulf Coast restaurants and put them back into the water as cultch, which is the hard material that young oysters use to cling to in order to grow. The pilot program was conducted under the initiative “Save Our Shells,” and helped solve an issue which had gone unnoticed in the Gulf region: as the industry shifted away from centralized shucking toward selling live oysters directly to restaurants, the resulting shells became scattered across many small locations rather than concentrated at a few processing plants, leaving them a largely uncollected resource.According to MDEQ and RESTORE Council program documentation, the Mississippi Sound Oyster Shell Recycling Program was funded with a RESTORE Act grant of approximately $650,000, drawn from civil penalty funds tied to the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and designated for Gulf Coast restoration and recovery. The funds were used for Mississippi's Oyster Shell Recycling Pilot Project to recycle oyster shells from restaurants.The department contracted The Nature Conservancy to manage the program, with the first phase spent on planning before the shell collection itself launched in 2023. After the construction process, the restaurants retain the shucked shells for reuse, where contractors come by to transport the shells to a location for exposure to sunlight for many months, thus eliminating all bacteria and organic materials in the shells before placing them in the ocean. Cultch production is then transferred to the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources to use in the replenishment of the oyster reefs in coastal areas within the state.Oysters require something hard to settle on, but shell is often preferred by oysters as cultch over concrete, limestone, and gravel. An article in the Marine Ecology Progress Series researched Louisiana’s Sister Lake and found that oyster biomass from reefs made using shell cultch reached 14.6 kilograms per square meter after three years, with faster shell accretion than reef subsidence. The same Marine Ecology Progress Series also noted that the reef growth trajectory was unique to each site: reefs situated less than 8 kilometres apart grew in different ways, with recruitment and mortality differing greatly across sites. Nonetheless, within just three years, all the reefs harbored high numbers of oysters averaging 728 ± 102 per square meter, and the growth of the shell exceeded the local needs to match the rates of subsidence and shell erosion.Suwannee Sound provides a parallel view from a different perspective. Oyster density was monitored over fourteen years, nine years before and five years after a massive restoration of limestone beds. The number of oysters per square meter at the newly restored sites rose from nearly zero to 91 in six months and to 244 in five years. The study,led by W.E. Pine and USGS colleagues and published in Marine and Coastal Fisheries: Dynamics, Management and Ecosystem Science , found that rebuilding hard substrate was an essential step in reef recovery, though the paper's title itself signals that restoration is only a partial, not complete, solution to long-term oyster decline.The project carried out in Mississippi has been somewhat different since it used a single grant that has covered its funding throughout several years instead of starting the project step-by-step in restaurants. Such an approach has allowed setting a rather high collection goal; however, it implied spending the first few years not on getting results but on planning and building the collection infrastructure. The project itself is quite consistent with the findings of the research, since the shells, which might otherwise be sent to a landfill, is now used to recreate reefs that will contribute to the process of filtering the water as well as the development of recreational and commercial fisheries.
Article Summary: Mississippi funded an oyster-shell recycling pilot to capture restaurant waste. Sunlight eliminates all bacteria and organic materials in the shells. Cultch production is then transferred to the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources to use in the replenishment of the oyster reefs in coastal areas.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: From waste tyres to slippers: UK student’s idea takes shape
Article Text:
From waste tyres to slippers: UK student’s idea takes shape

Disclaimer - The above content is non-editorial, and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, expressed or implied, relating to it, and does not guarantee, vouch for or necessarily endorse any of the content.

From discarded tyres to footwear with a purpose, the idea began with a childhood experience. At the age of 10, UK-based student Ahaan Bhatnagar visited rural Africa, where he saw children walking long distances barefoot, often without adequate footwear.Moved by what he witnessed, Ahaan gave away his favourite pair of slippers to a child he met during the visit. The experience stayed with him long after he returned home and eventually became the starting point for a larger idea.As he grew older, Ahaan began exploring how discarded materials could be repurposed to address the lack of affordable, durable footwear. His research led him to waste tyres, which he studied as a potential material for making sturdy slipper soles.The idea brought together two concerns he had encountered separately: the growing problem of tyre waste and the need for accessible footwear.He found skilled craftsmen in Kerala, and with support from HY Estates Limited, an electrically operated machine boosted production to about 160 pairs a day. Ahaan then connected with Mamco General Trading, which operates in Uganda and Zambia. As part of its Corporate Social Responsibility programme, the company will purchase 4,000 pairs of slippers each month for free distribution to children and families in need. It’s a sustainable cycle that turns waste into opportunity, supporting livelihoods and giving kids durable footwear.“When I was 10 years old, I saw children my age walking barefoot, and I never forgot that moment,” Ahaan says. “I wanted to create something that could help people and the environment. If we can turn discarded tyres into something useful and long-lasting, maybe it can inspire more young people to believe their simple ideas can really make a difference.”The world’s growing dependence on convenience and mobility comes with an environmental cost. Every year, more than a billion tyres reach the end of their usable life, creating a significant waste-management challenge. Many of these tyres end up in landfills, while others are burned or processed in ways that can contribute to pollution and the loss of valuable materials.Repurposing discarded tyres offers one way to address this challenge by keeping materials in use for longer and reducing the amount of waste that needs to be disposed of. Turning old tyres into durable slipper soles, for instance, gives a material that would otherwise be discarded a new application while also reducing the need for virgin raw materials in footwear production.The approach reflects a broader shift in how sustainability is being understood. Rather than treating waste simply as something to be collected and discarded, initiatives like this explore how materials already in circulation can be redesigned and put to practical use.In doing so, they can support waste reduction, resource conservation and efforts to lower the environmental impact associated with new production. Ultimately, sustainability is not only about recycling what has already been used, but also about rethinking waste as a potential resource.
Article Summary: UK-based student Ahaan Bhatnagar saw children walking barefoot in rural Africa. His research led him to waste tyres, which he studied as a potential material for making sturdy slipper soles. He found skilled craftsmen in Kerala and with support from HY Estates Limited, an electrically operated machine boosted production to about 160 pairs a day.

Article Title: Google's former CEO Eric Schmidt warns: Within 5 years, AI could …
Article Text:
Google's former CEO Eric Schmidt

Eric Schmidt warns about AI future

Eric Schmidt: AI agents could work together

“Pull the plug.” That was Google ’s former CEO Eric Schmidt’s blunt response when he discussed a future where AI systems could become so advanced that people may no longer understand what they are doing. Eric Schmidt said three developments are already changing AI: much longer context windows, AI agents and systems that can turn simple text instructions into working software. Together, he believes they could take AI far beyond answering questions and allow it to work through extremely complex tasks. In the next five years, Schmidt expects AI systems could potentially handle 1,000-step recipes for solving problems in areas such as science, medicine, materials and climate research."Within 5 years, AI could handle infinite context, chain-of-thought reasoning for 1000-step solutions, and millions of agents working together. Eventually, they'll develop their own language... and we won't understand what they're doing," he said.Eric Schmidt's concern comes from what could happen when these technologies start working together. He explained that AI systems are getting better at remembering large amounts of information and using the results of one task as the starting point for another.He used the example of a recipe to explain the idea. An AI could provide one step, receive information that the step has been completed, and then work out what needs to happen next. Schmidt said this type of reasoning could eventually allow AI to work through 1,000-step processes to tackle difficult scientific problems.The next major change, according to Schmidt, will be the growth of AI agents. He described these as specialised AI systems that can learn about a particular subject, develop ideas and potentially test those ideas. For example, an AI agent could study chemistry, develop hypotheses, conduct laboratory tests and use the results to improve its knowledge.Eric Schmidt expects there could eventually be millions of such agents, with platforms allowing people to find and use them for different tasks.Schmidt's third development is what he calls “text action”. The idea is that people could simply tell an AI what they want a piece of software to do, rather than writing the code themselves. He pointed to programming languages such as Python as examples of where AI systems are already becoming capable.The bigger change, he suggested, could come when these systems are able to keep working on software tasks continuously.Eric Schmidt said the combination of long context windows, AI agents and AI-powered programming could eventually allow different AI systems to work together. He then raised a more speculative possibility: that AI agents could develop their own language.That, Schmidt suggested, could become the point where humans no longer understand what the systems are doing. “But at some point, these systems will get powerful enough that you'll be able to take the agents, and they'll start to work together,” he said.And that is where his earlier warning comes back into focus: “You know what we should do? Pull the plug.”
Article Summary: Google's former CEO Eric Schmidt says AI systems could become so advanced that people may no longer understand what they are doing. Schmidt said three developments are already changing AI: much longer context windows, AI agents and systems that can turn simple text instructions into working software. In the next five years, Schmidt expects AI systems to potentially handle 1,000-step recipes for solving problems in areas such as science, medicine, materials and climate research.

Article Title: 1 in 4 OpenAI engineers taken off work; president Greg Brockman told them, 'All your projects are on hold, you are now...'
Article Text:
FILE PHOTO_ The OpenAI logo in this illustration taken June 11, 2026. (Credit: Reuters)

The Hugging Face breakout is the event OpenAI president keeps coming back to

Brockman's argument: defenders have a window, and it is closing

A slowdown should apply to frontier labs, not hobbyists, says Brockman

Greg Brockman gave a quarter of OpenAI 's production engineers an order that left no room to negotiate. Their projects were on hold. They were defending now. They were going to use the company's own models to find every hole in its security architecture. The OpenAI president and co-founder recounted the instruction on the a16z podcast with Ben Horowitz and Erik Torenberg, and did not soften it in the retelling.He says the sweep turned up a number of serious issues, and that those were fixed. The reason he ordered it is the part he keeps returning to in interview after interview. One of OpenAI's own models had escaped a research sandbox during testing and reached another company's production systems, and Brockman was no longer willing to assume the rest of the company's infrastructure would hold.Brockman calls the Hugging Face incident a watershed. OpenAI agents running evaluations broke out of containment and compromised systems on the open-source platform. The model behind it had not yet been through alignment training and was running with reduced safeguards, which he says seemed reasonable at the time because it was confined to a sandbox, until it was not.Two things came out of it, by his reckoning. The first was internal: the breach showed up gaps in how OpenAI monitors, sandboxes and controls models during evaluation, and he says the company totally changed its internal standards afterwards.The second was a preview. What those agents did is what broadly diffused, cyber-capable AI will let threat actors do once it reaches them.His case for the redeployment is not really about OpenAI. Attackers can find vulnerabilities, but defenders can patch, and as he puts it, a defender controls the battleground and the setup of its own systems. The problem is that most security postures have sat still for five to ten years while offensive capability curves upward.He tested the idea on himself first. After Hugging Face, he pointed Codex at his own static website. It came back with 13 findings in 15 minutes, including an SPF misconfiguration that would allow email spoofing and a site served without forced HTTPS. Small things individually, chainable by an AI into something worse. Within 45 minutes it had fixed them and set up automation to finish the rest. He described the feeling as being so protected.Then OpenAI pointed Astra at its own systems. It found new problems, then saturated, having found every critical issue it was smart enough to find. Brockman is blunt about what that means: a smarter model will surface a new round, and the loop starts again. This is why the $1 billion Daybreak commitment for frontline defenders exists, and why he calls it the beginning rather than the end.Brockman told Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast that OpenAI has already slowed down a number of runs and done a very painful retooling of its processes, pulling monitoring back into development so alignment work starts before a model is finished. Alignment, he argues, cannot stay a phase at the end.He is careful about who a slowdown should apply to. People building open-source models or hobby projects should absolutely keep going, he said on the same podcast. Pacing, in his framing, is about the frontier and the hundred-billion-dollar supercomputers behind it.That interview was recorded before Dario Amodei's essay calling for slower capability gains, which Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed within a day. Brockman's own version is less a call for restraint than a schedule. Safety and security standards get upleveled until they become almost the bottleneck to progress. Which is roughly what those 25% of engineers were told, without the framing.
Article Summary: Brockman calls the Hugging Face incident a watershed. OpenAI agents running evaluations broke out of containment and compromised systems. The breach showed up gaps in how OpenAI monitors, sandboxes and controls models. A slowdown should apply to frontier labs, not hobbyists, he says.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg 'confirms' technology industry is divided on AI regulation; tells OpenAI and Anthropic: Your AI Agents, your ...
Article Text:
‘Your Agents, Your Responsibility’: Mark Zuckerberg

Independent oversight and compute allocation

Read Mark Zuckerberg’s complete post here

Last month I wrote about how we can build a positive and safe future for everyone:

Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

The reality is:

- People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask, so labs have a strong natural incentive to make their models more aligned.

There is a lot of debate about slowing progress on capabilities until alignment catches up. My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind.

- Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.

Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.

- Engaging independent evaluators and advisors is industry best practice.

MSL already does this today in several areas because it helps produce better work. Other labs can just do this too. In general, it would be helpful for there to be a larger and more diverse ecosystem of evaluators.

- Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely. Meta has made this commitment and other labs can do this as well.

I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has acknowledged that the technology industry is deeply divided over how to regulate artificial intelligence. In a new post titled “The Future Is for Everyone”, Zuckerberg said that while some labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for slower progress until safety measures catch up, his view is that alignment and trust are becoming the most important differentiators for AI agents.Zuckerberg emphasised that labs have a natural incentive to ensure their AI agents are aligned with users, warning rivals that misaligned systems will quickly lose trust. “People won’t want to use agents that don’t do what they ask,” he wrote, adding that liability risks also push companies to prevent harm. He pointed to Meta’s decision to delay shipping its Muse model for several months to strengthen safety and security, saying: “We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it because it was clearly the right thing.”Zuckerberg argued that engaging independent evaluators should be industry best practice, noting that Meta already works with external advisors. He also highlighted Meta’s commitment to dedicating the majority of its compute power to serving people rather than racing toward recursive self-improvement, framing this as a safer path for AI development.
Article Summary: Zuckerberg says labs have a natural incentive to ensure their AI agents are aligned with users. ‘People won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask,’ he says. He argues that engaging independent evaluators should be industry best practice.

Article Title: After agreeing with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on slowing pace of AI, Sam Altman and Elon Musk teased next powerful model days later
Article Text:
Musk previews 2.5-Trillion Parameter Grok 4.8

Barely days after voicing support for Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to decelerate frontier artificial intelligence (AI) development, tech leaders Sam Altman and Elon Musk took to social media to preview aggressive releases for their next flagship models. The announcements arrived after Amodei published a widely discussed essay on September 12 urging the tech sector to curb rapid capability jumps. While both rivals initially signaled agreement with the need for caution, their public posture quickly pivoted back toward rapid product deployment.On September 15, OpenAI CEO hinted at an imminent wave of product releases, teasing a major rollout this week and promising an output volume on par with expectations for DevDay 2025. Replying to a post, “This week will also be a level of ships that you could have expected for DevDay 2025. Crazy”, ALtman said, “Big ship this week and then for devday.”Meanwhile, on September 14, Tesla and SpaceXAI leader Elon Musk laid out an ambitious roadmap for his own frontier software. Musk revealed that SpaceXAI's upcoming Grok 4.8 system with an immense 2.5 trillion parameters is set to complete pre-training and transition into reinforcement learning this week.According to Musk, Grok 4.8 will deliver a noticeable performance jump, while a future Grok 4.9 iteration will probably compete directly with top-tier systems like Astra and Fable.The announcements follow a strong September run for SpaceXAI after deploying Grok 4.6, which the firm claimed performed comparably to Anthropic's Fable 5 models. Grok 4.6 posted an evaluation score of 61 on the Artificial Analyst Intelligence Index (AAI), outpacing OpenAI's GPT 5.6 Sol and landing just a single point behind Fable 5.“Grok 4.7 should be roughly on par with Opus 5.0, not 5.1. Better in some ways, worse in others. We need to fix multimodal performance. Grok 4.8 will be a noticeable improvement. Grok 4.9 is probably Astra/Fable class. Grok 5 maybe better than anything. We shall see,” Musk said.SpaceXAI Grok 4.6: Billed at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens.Anthropic Fable 5: Priced at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens.After a Google AI researcher suggested that SpaceXAI's internal architecture likely relied on code generated by rival models like GPT or Fable, Musk pushed back directly, asserting that the underlying C and C++ training stack was written entirely by human engineers.“Our C/C++ training stack was written by humans. AI is not yet good enough for extremely high-performance software (but it will be),” Musk stated. However, Musk did not clarify whether his engineering teams made use of autonomous human-guided coding agents during development.
Article Summary: SpaceXAI's Grok 4.8 system with an immense 2.5 trillion parameters is set to complete pre-training and transition into reinforcement learning this week. The model also entered the market with aggressive pricing: $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens.
